items.title: 9.7.1 Calculating the pH of a buffer

blocks.text: To prepare a buffer of definite pH, consider a weak acid HA and its salt NaA with a strong base such as NaOH. The dissociations are HA gives H+ + A- and NaA gives Na+ + A-. The pH of the buffer is given by Henderson's equation: pH = pKa - log([acid] / [salt]), or, interchanging numerator and denominator so that the sign of the log changes, pH = pKa + log([salt] / [acid]). Two factors therefore govern the pH of a buffer: the pKa of the acid used, and the ratio of the concentrations of the salt and the acid. The best buffer is prepared by taking equal concentrations of salt and acid, so that the pH is controlled by the pKa of the acid. For the acetic acid-sodium acetate buffer with [CH3COOH] = [CH3COONa], pH = pKa + log 1 = pKa + 0 = pKa = 4.74: the pH of this buffer is just equal to the pKa of the acid. The body's blood buffering system, involving bicarbonates, helps maintain the pH of blood.

blocks.title: Henderson's equation
blocks.text: pH = pKa + log([salt] / [acid]); with equal salt and acid, pH = pKa.
A buffer is 0.50 M HF and 0.45 M fluoride, Ka of HF = 6.8 x 10^-4. Find its pH before and after adding 0.40 g NaOH to 1.0 dm3.
